title: Speed on an Elliptical Orbit
short: v² = GM(2/r − 1/a) gives the speed anywhere on an ellipse, which plans transfer orbits.
trouble: Students think a rocket burn changes the height of the orbit right where the burn happens, rather than on the far side.

blocks.html: On an elliptical orbit (Ellipses), the speed changes all the way around. Orbital Energy and Kepler's Second Law from Angular Momentum give one formula for the speed anywhere, and it is the tool for planning trips between planets. Try transfers in the Orbit Lab.

At the nearest point $r_p$ and farthest point $r_a$ the velocity is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, so angular momentum gives $r_pv_p = r_av_a$. Energy gives $\tfrac{1}{2}v_p^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r_p} = \tfrac{1}{2}v_a^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r_a}$ (per kilogram). Substituting $v_a = v_pr_p/r_a$ and solving, the total energy per kilogram comes out as $-\dfrac{GM}{r_p + r_a} = -\dfrac{GM}{2a}$, where $a = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_p + r_a)$ is the semi-major axis. Energy is the same everywhere on the orbit, so at any distance $r$: $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 - \dfrac{GM}{r} = -\dfrac{GM}{2a}$.

The vis-viva equation: $$v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right).$$ For a circle ($r = a$) it gives $v^2 = GM/r$. A Hohmann transfer between circular orbits $r_1$ and $r_2$ uses an ellipse with $a = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_1 + r_2)$: one burn at $r_1$ to get onto it, a second at $r_2$ to circularize.

blocks.name: ph-orbit

opts.task: Follow the transfer from Earth's orbit to Mars's: one burn to leave, half an orbit of coasting, one burn to arrive.

blocks.cap: A Hohmann transfer from Earth's orbit (1 AU) to Mars's (1.52 AU): the burn at Earth raises the far side of the orbit, half a revolution away.

blocks.title: Leaving Earth's orbit for Mars
blocks.q: A Hohmann transfer to Mars has $a = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + 1.524) = 1.262\ \text{AU}$. How fast must a craft move at 1 AU to be on it, compared with Earth's orbital speed? ($GM_\odot = 1.327 \times 10^{20}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$, $1\ \text{AU} = 1.496 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}$.)
steps: On the transfer orbit at $r = 1\ \text{AU}$: $v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{1\ \text{AU}} - \dfrac{1}{1.262\ \text{AU}}\right)$, so $v = 32.7\ \text{km/s}$.
The craft needs about $2.9\ \text{km/s}$ beyond Earth's orbital speed (on top of escaping Earth itself).

blocks.title: Up to geostationary orbit
blocks.q: A satellite at $r_1 = 6.671 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ (300 km up) transfers to $r_2 = 4.216 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}$. Find the first burn. (Earth: $GM = 3.986 \times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.)
steps: First burn: $10.16 - 7.73 = 2.43\ \text{km/s}$. (A second burn of about $1.47\ \text{km/s}$ at the top circularizes the orbit.)

blocks.html: Expecting a burn to change the orbit's height right where it happens. Right after a short burn the craft is still at the same place, so that point stays on the new orbit. What changes is the energy, and with it $a$: the far side of the orbit, half a revolution later, rises or falls. Check with vis-viva: at the burn point $r$ is fixed, so a bigger $v$ means a bigger $a$, and the opposite end, at $2a - r$, moves out.
